## Conclusion: The Evidence Says **Yes**, Not No

Contrary to your expectation, the available scientific evidence suggests that olive leaf extract **can** modestly reduce high blood pressure. Here is what the research shows:

**Key Clinical Trial (Susalit et al., 2011):** A double-blind, randomized, active-controlled study published in *Phytomedicine* compared olive leaf extract (500 mg twice daily) with the drug captopril in patients with stage-1 hypertension. Olive leaf extract significantly reduced both systolic and diastolic blood pressure, with effectiveness comparable to captopril at its standard dose. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/))

**2025 Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis:** A meta-analysis published in *Phytotherapy Research* (May 2025) pooled data from multiple RCTs and found that olive leaf extract supplementation was associated with meaningful reductions in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in pre-hypertensive and hypertensive individuals. ([Wiley/PTR](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ptr.8509); [NutraIngredients coverage](https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2025/05/15/olive-leaf-extract-may-support-healthy-blood-pressure/))

**Pooled Estimate:** A summary of 5 trials involving 325 adults reported a mean systolic blood pressure reduction of approximately 5.8 mmHg with 500 mg/day olive leaf extract over at least 8 weeks versus control. ([Verus PhytoMed](https://www.verusphytomed.com/olive-leaf-extract-reference))

**Caveats:** The reductions are modest, sample sizes across trials are relatively small, and olive leaf extract should not replace prescribed antihypertensive medications without medical supervision. However, the evidence consistently points toward a real blood-pressure-lowering effect rather than no effect.

In short, the answer to your question appears to be **yes** — olive leaf extract does show evidence of reducing high blood pressure, though the effect is modest and not a substitute for standard treatment.
